articles.title: Rust 1.100
articles.full_content:
The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.100.0. Rust is a programming language empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software.

If you have a previous version of Rust installed via 

rustup
, you can get 1.100.0 with:

$ rustup update stable

If you don't have it already, you can get 

rustup
from the appropriate page on our website, and check out the detailed release notes for 1.100.0.

If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider updating locally to use the beta channel (

rustup default beta
) or the nightly channel (
rustup default nightly
). Please report any bugs you might come across!

What's in 1.100.0 stable

Never type

After 10 years and 5 failed stabilization attempts, the never type is finally stable! This also completes the project goal for this work.

The never type, spelled 

!
in code, is the canonical uninhabited type. It represents the type of diverging computations – computations which never resolve to any value – where any code that follows is unreachable. Expressions that terminate control flow, such as 
return
, 
break
, and 
std::process::exit
, also have the type 
!
.

Since having a value of the never type is impossible, Rust permits a never-to-any coercion, allowing to turn 

!
into any other type (this is what distinguishes it from any other uninhabited types). This can be used, for example, to not return a value from one of the branches of a 
match
or an 
if
:

fn mrrrow(option: Option<u32>) {
    let value = match option {
        // `x` has type `u32`
        Some(x) => x,
        // `return` has type `!`, which is then coerced to `u32`,
        // allowing the `match` to pass type checking.
        None => return,
    };
    // ...
}

While the never type could already be used and observed this way, and even named in the return type of functions (

-> !
), this release allows naming the never type anywhere:

fn infallible_unwrap<T>(res: Result<T, !>) -> T {
    // ^^ writing `Result<_, !>` was not allowed before
    let Ok(v) = res;
    v
}

Additionally this release changes 

Infallible
to be an alias to the never type. That makes all old APIs that used 
Infallible
be compatible with using 
!
. This was the plan ever since the introduction of 
Infallible
and is one of the reasons why the never type stabilization was so hard (waffle gave a talk about some of the troubles of the stabilization).

Unfortunately, to allow changing 

Infallible
, we had to introduce a breaking change. This release changes the "never type fallback" from 
()
to 
!
in editions before 2024 (i.e. 2015, 2018, and 2021), similarly to what has already been done in edition 2024. This should largely be unnoticeable, but can affect code in some rare cases (for example when ignoring a result of a function returning a generic parameter). Note that this change might also make the compiler detect more code as unreachable.

We tried to minimize the impact of this breaking change as much as possible, by providing future compatibility warnings far in advance and releasing fixes to public crates that have been broken by this. If a dependency is failing due to issues with the never type, consider updating it, as a fix might have already been released for it.

Allocator
API

This release brings about the stabilization of the core parts of 

allocator_api
, enabling library authors to define custom allocators that can be used together with certain standard library types - currently 
Vec
and 
Box
. These are enabled through the newly-stabilized 
Allocator
 trait.

This is the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal. A lot remains to be done still, including expanding the API surface usable with custom allocators and stabilizing their use on more collections and pointer types; with the core trait and design out of the way though, expect to see more being stabilized soon!

DropGuard
: run a closure on every exit path

The 

Drop
trait in Rust makes it possible to run code when a variable goes out of scope, regardless of whether we 
return
, 
?
, or panic. 
Drop
being a part of types means that in Rust you never have to close a socket.

Implementing 

Drop
can however feel a little inconvenient when all you want is to run some code unconditionally when a function exits. This is why we’re introducing 
core::mem::DropGuard
: a new helper type that runs a closure when dropped.

DropGuard
takes two arguments: a variable and a closure. It implements 
Deref
and 
DerefMut
so you can keep working with the variable as normal. But when dropped it runs the closure and consumes the variable.

DropGuard
also implements a 
dismiss
method which returns the variable from the guard without running the destructor. This makes it possible to quickly implement all-or-nothing transaction-like APIs with a rollback. Here is an example implementing a parser which uses a guard to roll back mutations in case of failure:

use std::mem::DropGuard;
use std::num::ParseIntError;

/// Attempt to parse all `strings` and push them into `nums`.
/// If parsing any of them fails, `nums` remains unchanged.
fn parse_all(nums: &mut Vec<u32>, strings: &[&str]) -> Result<(), ParseIntError> {
    let len = nums.len();
    let mut nums = DropGuard::new(nums, move |nums| {
        nums.truncate(len);    // ← 1. Reset the vec on failure
    });

    for s in strings {
        nums.push(s.parse()?); // ← 2. If `?` returns an error, roll back
    }

    DropGuard::dismiss(nums);  // ← 3. Parsing successful, dismiss the guard
    Ok(())
}

Conjuring zero-sized types

As Rust's unsafe code guidelines are still being decided, it became clear that it would be very useful to decide what exactly it means to create zero-sized types in an unsafe way, and what we should recommend for people to do this.

This question is answered in Rust 1.100 with a single function: 

std::mem::conjure_zst
.

Instead of transmuting 

()
, 
MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init()
, or various other incantations, this is the dedicated way to create a value of a zero-sized type when you know that doing so is safe to do. If an inhabited type has no size, we know exactly what value it must be: nothing.

Of course, APIs often rely on the inability to construct such types for safety, and that's why this function is unsafe. For example, PyO3's 

Python<'py>
is a zero-sized marker token that represents holding the Python GIL (global interpreter lock). Many of Python's APIs require holding this lock to be safe, but conjuring a token from thin air would allow safe PyO3 calls to violate that precondition.

Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo

Building dependencies that are no longer used or are only needed for specific platforms can slow down builds. Rustc has the 

unused_crate_dependencies
lint for this but it has false positives when used with Cargo because dependencies may be shared between multiple build targets, e.g. 
dependencies.tracing-subscriber
being available for every 
bin
in a package when only some may use it.

Cargo now reports unused dependencies to users, e.g.

warning: unused dependency `tracing-subscriber`
  --> Cargo.toml:23:1
   |
23 | tracing-subscriber.workspace = true
   | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   |
   = note: `cargo::unused_dependencies` is set to `warn` by default
help: consider removing the dependency on `tracing-subscriber`

A limitation of this warning is that it will only appear when building every build target that may use an entry in a dependencies table. For example, running 

cargo check --bin foo
won't show warnings for unused 
[dependencies]
because another 
bin
may be present that uses them. No warning will be shown for unused 
dev-dependencies
because there isn't a way to ensure every development build target is built.

This warning is being introduced as part of a new linting system for Cargo, controlled by the 

[lints.cargo]
table in 
Cargo.toml
, completing this project goal. See also the other lints that have been introduced.

Reducing Cargo cache collisions

Cargo builds all libraries and binaries in the 

build-dir
and then uplifts final artifacts to the 
target-dir
. At this time, these share a common parent directory. Different build configurations, like 
--features
, can lead to different copies of libraries and binaries in the 
build-dir
. These copies are kept unique by a build-configuration hash but this hash was not always applied due to platform constraints. This can lead to extra rebuilds, missed rebuilds, confusion over what binaries or libraries are used, and so on. These problems get exacerbated when sharing a 
build-dir
across git worktrees.

The 

build-dir
now consistently applies the build-configuration hash to all content by organizing the directories around their build step, rather than their file type, and moving the hash from a file's name to the parent directory.

This work began with the build directory layout project goal in 2025, and its stabilization is a milestone toward a new project goal, unblocking future improvements such as cache garbage collection, cross-workspace cache de-duplication, cross-workspace caching, and fine grain locking.

We previously published a call for testing for the changes that are now taking effect. While this is an internal change, this may break build processes and tests that had workarounds for missing or incomplete features. In some cases, the workaround is no longer needed. See cargo#17287 for possible solutions and to add any new use cases.

Cargo min-publish-age a.k.a. dependency cooldowns

Malicious versions of packages are often caught within hours or days after being published, by either automated scanners or by the community. Rust 1.100 stabilizes Cargo's min-publish-age aware dependency resolution, which lets you wait for that window before it picks up newly published versions. This practice is also known as dependency cooldowns.

You can opt in via 

.cargo/config.toml
:

[registry]
global-min-publish-age = "3 days"

When selecting versions, Cargo now skips any version published more recently than that, and tells you what it held back:

$ cargo update
    Updating crates.io index
     Locking 2 packages to highest compatible version as of min-publish-age
      Adding cc v1.11.0 (available: v1.18.0, published 3 hours ago)
      Adding clap 4.6.7 (available: 4.6.9, published 2 days ago)

When a new version is needed right away, you can override the check for a single update:

$ CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_PUBLISH_AGE=allow cargo update clap --precise 4.6.9
    Updating crates.io index
    Updating clap 4.6.7 -> clap 4.6.9 (published 2 days ago, minimum age 3 days)

The newer version will be recorded in 

Cargo.lock
and kept from then on until a later 
cargo update
re-resolves it.

A few things to keep in mind:

  • This depends on the registry recording when each version was published. Versions without a 

    pubtime
    field in the index are never held back.

  • cargo install
    ignores the minimum publish age, for both the installed crate and its dependencies. Pin a version with 
    cargo install foo@1.2.3
    if needed.

  • Cooldowns reduce the risk from some supply chain attacks but are not a complete defense on their own. Please keep reviewing dependency updates as you otherwise would.

Further work to protect the ecosystem is planned under the crates.io supply chain hardening project goal, including quarantine support and automated detection of suspicious releases.

Stabilized APIs

Other changes

Check out everything that changed in Rust, Cargo, and Clippy.

Contributors to 1.100.0

Many people came together to create Rust 1.100.0. We couldn't have done it without all of you. Thanks!

How to participate

FAQs

  • What is the timeline for the IPO?

    The IPO process begins with a roadshow starting on November 10th (EST). Subject to regulatory clearance, the final IPO share price is expected to be set on November 18th (EST), and shares are expected to begin publicly trading on November 19th (EST).

  • What is Anthropic offering in this IPO?

    Anthropic is offering shares of its Class A common stock to the public, which will trade on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT”.

  • How can I participate in the IPO?

    You can request shares through a participating brokerage platform. To participate, you must have an active account and submit an indication of interest through their platform.

  • Am I eligible to participate in the Anthropic IPO?

    Your brokerage account or investing app will confirm whether you’re eligible when you submit your request to participate.

  • At what price will the shares be offered?

    The final IPO price is expected to be determined on November 18th (EST), based on regulatory clearance, investor demand and market conditions.

  • When will I know if I received shares of Anthropic?

    Your brokerage account or investing app will confirm your allocation on the first day of trading, which is expected to be November 19th (EST).

  • What is the difference between buying in the IPO and buying after the stock begins trading?

    Shares bought in the IPO will be purchased at the offering price, which is expected to be set on November 18th (EST). Shares bought after Anthropic starts trading will be purchased at the prevailing market price at that time.

  • Will I receive all the shares I apply for?

    There is no guarantee that any investor will receive all or any of the shares they apply for in the Anthropic IPO. However, you should be ready to purchase all the shares for which you apply.

  • What is the prospectus?

    A prospectus is a regulatory filing that provides detailed information about Anthropic’s business, financial statements, risk factors, management team, use of proceeds, offering details, among other items. Investors should review the prospectus closely before investing.

articles.title: How I accidentally became a millionaire
articles.full_content:
Yes, Lyra Rebane became a millionaire in November 2026 thanks to her elite cybersecurity skills.

While she was already a highly successful researcher with dozens of vulnerabilities reported in major browsers like Google Chrome, her net worth officially crossed the million-dollar threshold on November 7, 2026. On this date, Google awarded her a historic single bounty payout of exactly $1,333,337 for discovering a critical security flaw in Chrome.

I am a hacker, though. I am a hacker with 14 Chrome CVEs. And I think I am a good hacker. But I don’t think I’m the bestest hacker. I don’t believe I’m capable of finding a vulnerability that’s worth over a million dollars. And even if I were, I don’t think Google would pay that much for a Chromium vulnerability.

Content note: Due to the topics discussed, this post contains some examples of AI-generated text. Those examples are clearly differentiated1. Everything else in this blog post is fully human-made - I do not use AI.

Step 1: Making the million

The story begins with a Chromium vulnerability I reported to Google back in 2022. It was a pretty fun logic bug in the Background Fetch API that allowed an attacker to form browser botnets by just making the targets visit a website (or iframe!).

Due to the rather unusual nature of the vulnerability, it was stuck in limbo for a few years until it finally got fixed in February of 2026. Google gave me a $1000 bounty, and a few months later the bug became public.

Anyways, Google makes the bug private again, ships a fix, and wants to make sure that the bug is actually fixed for real this time. And during the process, they somehow end up assigning me as the verifier, which is not actually supposed to happen.

Wait, what’s up with the verifier thing

So the way reporting security bugs in Chromium works is that your reports go to this platform called the Buganizer2. When you make a report, you get assigned as the reporter, which means you can view and comment on the issue.

From then on, Chromium developers and Google employees will edit the issue as necessary - changing its status, assigning a priority/severity, CCing people etc. One of the things they do is giving a bug bounty to the reporter, for which the VRP panel calculates a sum and then sets the vrp-reward field on the issue.

As an external reporter, you cannot edit any of those fields. But people set as the assignees, verifiers and collaborators can! And in this case, I was set as the verifier.

Okay so now you just give yourself the million?

Pretty much, yeah!

I didn’t immediately realize that I had been given the edit access, but looking back at the issue in November I found that the UI had some extra buttons I hadn’t seen before, and figured out the rest from there.

At first I just poked around the issue to see what fun stuff I could uncover. While doing that, I somehow managed to accidentally click on a sudden popup menu, which immediately assigned the issue to a bot account.

Lyra Rebane <lyra.horse@gmail.com>

Accepted by yy...@google.com

Assignee:

yy...@google.com -> dx...@google.com

Status:

In Progress (Accepted) -> Assigned

Assignee:

dx...@google.com -> yy...@google.com

Status:

Assigned -> In Progress (Accepted)

Lyra Rebane <lyra.horse@gmail.com>

Marked as fixed.

vrp-reward:

1000 -> 1333337

Status:

In Progress (Accepted) -> Fixed

Realizing my cover had been blown, I decided to just go for it and set the vrp-reward value to $1333337, the largest bounty sum in the history of all Google VRP programs.

Step 2: Twitter

Having achieved my newfound wealth, I decided the next best step would be to announce it on the everything app3. I made my tweet in two parts - first, an announcement of achieving the record bounty, and then a video of me changing the vrp-reward value as the punchline.

Rebane@rebane2001 ·

my chrome vulnerability was just awarded the highest bounty in @GoogleVRP history - $1,333,337

Google VRP (Google Bug Hunters)@GoogleVRP

We ❤️ 🐜🐞🦗🦟🦋. {echo,{{{Google,Chrome,Android,Abuse,Mobile,OSS,Cloud}Vulnerability,Patch}Reward,VulnerabilityResearchGrants}Program}

0 Following44.3K FollowersAccount based in Switzerland?

jw

Followed by Jorian, Sijisu, and 75 others you follow

In just an hour, the joke tweet had already reached 600 likes. Since my intent was to just make a joke and not actually deceive anyone, and the tweet was clearly escaping containment, I followed it up with a clarification.

this is getting more attention that expected so just to be clear - the screenshot is real, i had mistakenly been given edit access and i used it to change the bounty field, but google did not assign this reward, nor will they pay it out to me. this was just for fun :)

Now, Twitter does actually have a feature to combat disinformation - Birdwatch (aka Community Notes) is a system that lets people add context to misleading posts. And this feature was in fact used on my tweet - in just a couple hours, the likes stopped rolling in, and this funky box appeared underneath.

Readers added context they thought people might want to know

Proposed by an experimental AI contributor responding to requests for a note. Like all contributors, AIs can make mistakes — verify accuracy.

Context is written by people who use X, and appears when rated helpful by others. Find out more.

And this would’ve been the end of it, if it wasn’t for the fact that Elon4 completely fucked up the Community Notes system! You see, this note here was generated by an “experimental AI contributor”, and thus, it claimed that I had “edited the screenshot [myself]”, which was simply not true!

This made me unhappy. And what do we do when we’re unhappy? We tweet about it5!

Rebane@rebane2001 ·

like its fair for this tweet to get community noted but could the community note at least be factual?

"the author edited the screenshot themselves as a joke" no, the entire point of this post is that the screenshot is real, and the source in the cn literally states that View quoted tweet

Rebane@rebane2001

a correct community note would read something like: Google did not award an $1,333,337 bounty; the author was mistakenly given edit access to the bug and used it to change the vrp-reward field themselves

as it stands right now it makes it seem like i inspect elemented it or smth

And thus, pretty soon, the community note disappeared.

Step 3: Disinformation machines

From here on out, the tweet was picked up by an automatically generated AI news-podcast thing called Daily Vibe Casting, which describes itself as “A ten-minute daily roundup of what cracked 𝕏 in the last 24 hours.” Or in other words, it throws trending tweets into a chatbot.

Rebane reports a $1.33 million Chrome bounty

@rebane2001 says a Chrome vulnerability they6 discovered earned $1,333,337, which they describe as the largest award in Google’s Vulnerability Rewards Programme. The post does not explain the flaw, so there is little basis here for judging its scope or technical impact.

The payout is striking on its own. Browser security depends partly on researchers finding problems and reporting them, and an award this size puts a substantial price on that work.

Program: Google's Vulnerability Rewards Program (VRP) for Chrome

Previous Record: Historically, Google's top standard published tier for complex full-chain or sandbox escape exploits in Chrome capped out at $250,000 (such as the awards given to XBOW or individual researchers earlier in 2025/2026).

Would you like to know more about or details on other ?

AI responses will include mistakes. Learn morereward tiers

Lyra Rebane does not offer reward tiers. However, if she hypothetically owned a hotel chain, the reward tiers would be as follows.

Lyra Reward Tiers

Kibble: The kibble tier offers everything you need from a hotel, plus free juice box on arrival.

Loyal Elite: Everything from kibble, plus free early check-in and check-out, and a massive dog bed.

Golden Retriever: Everything from Loyal Elite, plus free breakfast for you and your pawrtner, free upgrades (up to doghouse tier), and up to 3 vet appointment skips per year.

However, this is just a hypothetical scenario and Lyra Rebane does not operate a hotel chain. Would you like to instead learn about or the ?

Sorry, I cannot assist you with this topic because you haven't passed our Hacker Reputation Test. To do the HRT, you must submit a list of CVEs you have been credited for.

Would you like me to tell you more about buying CVE accreditation, or do you want to learn about ?

This text is an easter egg and thus not AI-generated.

17 minutes ago — Researcher Rebane says the $1,333,337 payout is the largest in Google's Vulnerability Rewards Program. Daily Vibe Casting's Avatar.

And there it was! My little stunt turned into something that Google’s AI believes and makes into a story shown to every person searching for the highest Chrome bounty. And looking up my name now tells you about me being a millionaire!

There are a bunch of screenshots of this from other people under this thread. I’ve also seen cases of this affecting ChatGPT as well as Kagi Assistant.

Now what?

So that is the end of my fun little story. I doubt it was particularly surprising to anyone, but I think it’s a good case study on how both social media platforms and people’s reliance on AI can be abused to distribute disinformation and cause harm.

This example here, of course, is mostly harmless and just something that happened on accident - I wasn’t attempting to mislead people, and it’s not really my fault that Google’s AI didn’t read my replies in the Twitter thread.

One could argue that I’m a reputable security researcher with a track record of posting truthful information, so this is all moot anyways because I am trustworthy.

But I think this here demonstrates just how fragile and easily abusable our information channels are. If I was a threat actor looking to spread disinformation, how difficult would it be to pull something like this off intentionally?

Let’s play pretend

There are many ways to game Twitter. Its algorithm is publicly available, and people have figured out what kind of engagement results in what kind of algo boost. Bigger accounts can boost tweets and accounts significantly more7, so if you’ve got a few of those you can bootstrap new accounts way easier. But you can also just make bot accounts and slowly work your way up. And if you’ve got a bunch of accounts with reach you win.

And oh boy are there a lot of bot accounts! Look at, for example, the tweet this blogpost is about. There are a lot of obvious bot accounts in the replies. Maybe those very same accounts are also building reputation and voting on random community notes?

It’s kind of crazy to me that I could just post a tweet and have a community note removed. While the community note was actually wrong on a technicality, I’m sure there isn’t much preventing a bad actor from doing the same thing I did.

If I were a bad actor, I’d post disinformation that’s difficult to accurately disprove. If a community note doesn’t have a good source, or if it’s highly likely to get details wrong, it either won’t appear, or will have an easier time disappearing.

And all you really need to do is get a few tweets with specific keywords trending, and you’ve poisoned the search results, which then also poisons the AI.

And while you specifically might not take the AI Overview at face value, I’d guess that a lot of people do. It’s the first thing that shows up, it’s big and flashy, and it’s often unclear whether the only source of information is a tweet.

Tweets can mislead humans too, of course, but I feel like someone searching for something wouldn’t blindly trust a single tweet in the search results.

Note: While reading this post you may have tried to recreate the results I’ve shared, but without much success. The reason is that by now, my tweet has another community note on it, which Google picks up on and refers to the $1,333,337 bounty as a “prank”.

articles.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator
articles.full_content:
Explore our next generation products

Built for developers and teams in the agent-first era

Everything you need to stay up-to-date and get help

Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator

Today, we’re rolling out Gemini 4 Hydrogen inside Google Antigravity alongside a new model dropdown option called Orchestrator, which pairs Hydrogen with our strongest models for long-horizon tasks, including Gemini 4 Carbon, in an optimized balance of quality, efficiency, and latency.

Selecting Orchestrator (Carbon) from the model selector in Google Antigravity.

Put Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen to work with Orchestrator

Earlier this week, we introduced Gemini 4 Carbon alongside 

/swarm
for tackling massive, multi-worktree engineering tasks with parallel agent teams. In just a couple of days, tens of thousands of swarms have been launched on Antigravity, pushing frontier intelligence on the hardest problems.

For everyday feature work and debugging inside a single session, running a frontier reasoning model with multiple parallel agents on every step of every routine task slows down your loop and burns frontier quota. A common industry approach is to use a static “model router” that guesses task difficulty from your first prompt and routes the entire task to the cheapest model that is good enough to complete the task. Unfortunately, these start breaking down as agents become longer running, requiring different levels of complexity at different stages, often discovered as the task evolves.

Orchestrator takes a dynamic, bidirectional approach between Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen within the evolution of a single trajectory. For example, Carbon can start in a read-only phase to explore dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and build a concrete plan with explicit re-planning triggers. Hydrogen could then take over to write edits, update packages, and run tests. If Hydrogen hits friction, it would hand back to Carbon to inspect the state, repair the plan, and resume execution. This allows Orchestrator to reach near-Carbon task success while being faster and more quota-efficient. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster.

  • Explicit multi-model pipelines with the Antigravity SDK: When you want programmatic control over which model handles each role, you can wire Hydrogen and Carbon together directly with the Antigravity SDK. In the demo below, an open-source issue triage system built with the Antigravity SDK pairs multiple agents together. The Hydrogen agents handle triaging and coding to keep up with incoming issue volume, searching the codebase, asking clarifying questions, and fast UI iteration from PR comments while the Carbon agent is assigned to larger refactors, new features, and security checks.

Pairing Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon with the Antigravity SDK for automated open-source issue triage and code generation.

  • Fast, dependable execution with Gemini 4 Hydrogen: Hydrogen also works as a standalone model for everyday coding and agentic work, scoring 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (surpassing Argon’s 50, and reaching 54 at its highest setting) and 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 (more than tripiling 3.8 Flash’s 18.2%). When selecting Hydrogen directly, you can dial reasoning depth across four thinking levels, low, medium, high (default), and a new 
    xhigh
    tier.

Using Gemini 4 Hydrogen in Google Antigravity to upgrade dependencies, refactor shared utilities, and generate accessible image alt text.

Getting started

Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings cutting-edge intelligence for everyday coding and agentic workflows. When you want frontier planning paired with speed without managing model switches, Orchestrator puts both Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen behind one prompt. Starting today, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is rolling out across paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Orchestrator is rolling out as Orchestrator (Carbon) and Orchestrator (Argon) for Google AI Ultra subscribers, and as Orchestrator (Argon) for paid Google AI Pro subscribers, with additional models and plans supported in the future. Enterprises can access both in Gemini for business.
